data_objects.name: subject_sensor_series
data_objects.meaning: Fifteen same-schema, per-subject time-series tables containing a session identifier, numeric sample time, and channels labeled EDA, heart rate, temperature, and blood volume pulse.

data_objects.name: survey_results
data_objects.meaning: A table of subject-associated time intervals with a coded stress-level response and 13 coded contextual-factor fields.

variables.name: session
variables.meaning: Session identifier string; sampled values have the form of the subject ID, an underscore, and a 10-digit integer.

variables.name: real_time
variables.meaning: Numeric sample time; sampled within-session sequences advance by 0.25 and the magnitude is consistent with an epoch-style timestamp.

variables.name: eda
variables.meaning: Electrodermal-activity measurement labeled EDA.

variables.name: hr
variables.meaning: Heart-rate measurement labeled HR.

variables.name: temp
variables.meaning: Temperature measurement.

variables.name: bvp
variables.meaning: Blood-volume-pulse measurement labeled BVP.

variables.name: ID
variables.meaning: Subject identifier; observed values match the subject tokens in the sensor filenames and session prefixes.

variables.name: Start time
variables.meaning: Start of the reported interval, encoded as YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS with no timezone field.

variables.name: End time
variables.meaning: End of the reported interval, encoded as YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS with no timezone field.

variables.name: Duration
variables.meaning: Recorded interval duration, encoded as HH:MM:SS.

variables.name: Date
variables.meaning: Calendar-date label associated with the interval, encoded as YYYY-MM-DD; it does not always equal the date portion of Start time.

variables.name: Stress level
variables.meaning: Coded stress-level response; observed codes are 0, 1, and 2.

variables.name: COVID related
variables.meaning: 0/1-coded survey field concerning whether the interval was COVID related.

variables.name: Treating a COVID patient
variables.meaning: 0/1-coded survey field concerning treatment of a COVID patient.

variables.name: Patient in crisis
variables.meaning: 0/1-coded survey field concerning a patient in crisis.

variables.name: Patients or their family
variables.meaning: 0/1-coded survey field concerning patients or their family.

variables.name: Doctors or colleagues
variables.meaning: 0/1-coded survey field concerning doctors or colleagues.

variables.name: Ancilliary services
variables.meaning: 0/1-coded survey field concerning ancillary services; the variable name preserves the source spelling.

variables.name: Increased workload
variables.meaning: 0/1-coded survey field concerning increased workload.

variables.name: Technology related stress
variables.meaning: 0/1-coded survey field concerning technology-related stress.

variables.name: Lack of supplies
variables.meaning: 0/1-coded survey field concerning lack of supplies.

variables.name: Documentation
variables.meaning: 0/1-coded survey field concerning documentation.

variables.name: Competency related stress
variables.meaning: 0/1-coded survey field concerning competency-related stress.

variables.meaning: 0/1-coded survey field concerning safety.

variables.meaning: 0/1-coded survey field concerning the work environment.

structure.description: The sensor object is horizontally consistent across 15 files: every file has the columns session, real_time, eda, hr, temp, and bvp. Each file is partitioned by the subject token in its filename, and one row represents one aligned set of channel values at one sample time within one session.

Sampled sensor files contain multiple session values. Within sampled contiguous runs, real_time is ordered and advances by 0.25 seconds, so the observed row grid is four rows per second; all four measurement channels share that row-level time coordinate.

The survey table contains 217 data rows. One row represents one subject-associated reported interval with start, end, duration, date, stress code, and contextual codes. Multiple rows may share an ID, and the rows are not globally ordered by Start time.

All 15 survey ID values have a corresponding subject sensor filename. The same ID also appears as the prefix of sampled session values, providing the explicit cross-object subject relationship; both objects contain repeated records per subject.

The objects expose a candidate temporal relationship between survey Start time/End time intervals and sensor real_time samples, but exact alignment depends on the undeclared epoch and timezone conventions. Date is an associated label rather than a reliable duplicate of the Start time calendar date.

uncertainties: The public files do not declare units for eda, hr, temp, or bvp; conventional domain units were therefore not assigned.
real_time has epoch-like magnitudes and quarter-second steps, but the epoch reference and timezone are not declared. Start time and End time also omit timezone information.
The semantic labels or ordering represented by Stress level codes 0, 1, and 2 are not defined in the public files.
The contextual fields are observed as 0/1 codes, but their response instructions, polarity, and treatment of nonresponse are not explicitly documented.
The meaning of the 10-digit suffix in session is not declared, and exhaustive uniqueness of session plus real_time was not established from bounded sampling.
No explicit missing-value token was observed in the bounded samples, but the public files do not state a missing-value convention.
Date can differ from the calendar date in Start time, particularly for overnight intervals, but its operational definition is not supplied.
annotation_notes: Evidence was restricted to the 16 CSV files under the declared public directory; no task, description, private, gold, grader, output, or prior-annotation artifacts were inspected.

Headers were checked across all 15 subject files. Content inspection was bounded to starts from five subject files, interior and tail samples from three differently sized subject files, and separated regions of survey_results.csv.
Field meanings are grounded in source headers, filename/session patterns, observed encodings, and cross-file ID coverage; unresolved domain definitions remain in uncertainties.
